top_level_objectives: Use a Lewis structure to count electron domains around a central atom.
Predict electron-domain geometry by minimizing repulsions among electron pairs.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.
Relate ideal and observed bond angles to the greater repulsion exerted by lone pairs.
Apply VSEPR predictions to common molecules in General Chemistry I.

scenes.scene_name: From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce how a 2D Lewis structure is translated into a count of electron domains around a central atom, establishing the input to VSEPR reasoning.
key_visuals: A flat Lewis structure of a simple central-atom molecule with bonding pairs and lone pairs highlighted in different colors
Electron domains appearing as grouped regions around the central atom rather than as individual bonds
A side-by-side view showing 2D notation transforming into a 3D domain model
student_actions: Identify the central atom in several example Lewis structures
Count bonding regions and lone-pair regions around the central atom
Classify each region as one electron domain before moving to 3D prediction

scenes.scene_name: Core VSEPR Principle: Domains Spread Out
scenes.brief_purpose: Show that electron domains arrange themselves to minimize mutual repulsion, leading to the five fundamental electron-domain geometries.
key_visuals: Movable electron domains around a central atom that repel one another and settle into stable arrangements
A sequence of domain counts from 2 to 6 producing linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements
Ideal bond angles displayed briefly with each arrangement
student_actions: Manipulate 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 electron domains around a central atom
Observe each set relax into its minimum-repulsion arrangement
Match each domain count to its electron-domain geometry name

scenes.scene_name: From Electron-Domain Geometry to Molecular Shape
scenes.brief_purpose: Distinguish the full electron-domain arrangement from the molecular geometry seen when lone pairs are omitted from the visible shape.
key_visuals: Pairs of models showing all electron domains first, then only atom positions for the molecular shape
Examples where the same electron-domain geometry produces different molecular geometries depending on lone-pair count
Highlighted lone-pair regions fading from view to reveal the named molecular geometry
student_actions: Hide lone pairs from a tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral domain arrangement
Name the resulting molecular geometries such as bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal, and square planar
Compare electron-domain geometry names with molecular geometry names for the same model

scenes.brief_purpose: Demonstrate that lone pairs repel more strongly than bonding pairs, causing bond-angle compression relative to ideal geometries.
key_visuals: A tetrahedral arrangement comparing methane and water, with lone-pair regions drawn larger than bonding regions
Animated bond angles narrowing as lone pairs are added
Numerical angle labels showing 109.5° for methane and 104.5° for water, with ammonia as an intermediate comparison
student_actions: Add lone pairs stepwise to a tetrahedral electron-domain arrangement
Observe how bond angles change as lone-pair repulsion increases
Explain why water and ammonia deviate from the ideal tetrahedral angle

scenes.scene_name: Five Parent Geometries and Their Common Derivatives
scenes.brief_purpose: Organize the common VSEPR shapes as families derived from the five fundamental electron-domain geometries.
key_visuals: A branching visual map from each parent geometry to its common molecular shapes
Representative examples for linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral families
Quick rotating 3D models of bent, trigonal pyramidal, seesaw, T-shaped, square pyramidal, and square planar
student_actions: Sort molecular shapes under the correct parent electron-domain geometry
Identify how many bonding pairs and lone pairs define each common shape
Use the family map to predict an unseen shape from a given domain count and lone-pair count

scenes.scene_name: Match VSEPR Predictions to Real Molecules
scenes.brief_purpose: Apply the full workflow to recognizable molecules and compare predicted structures with known examples from chemistry.
key_visuals: 3D models of water, ammonia, methane, PF5, SF6, and XeF4 displayed alongside their Lewis structures
Labels pairing each molecule with its electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry
A comparison panel showing idealized prediction and observed molecular shape agreement
student_actions: Start from each molecule’s Lewis structure and determine the electron-domain count
Predict both electron-domain geometry and molecular geometry for each molecule
Check predictions against the displayed real-molecule examples and reflect on patterns across the set
